newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians welcome ministers' offer to resign.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians welcome ministers' offer to resign.

text.p: Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip on Saturday welcomed an offer by 16 of President Yasser Arafat's ministers to resign but some said they were uncertain whether a reshuffle would take place.
All but two of Arafat's 18 ministers offered to quit at a cabinet meeting on Friday in the West Bank town of Ramallah after allegations of corruption and mismanagement by Palestinian legislators.
"Everything is now in the hands of President Arafat who is the only one who will take the right decision for the people," said Kamal Zewik, an engineer from the West Bank town of Hebron.
The gesture came as Arafat grapples with a peacemaking crisis with Israel after the killing of 13 people in central Jerusalem on Wednesday by two Islamist suicide bombers.
Arafat indicated on Saturday that he would not act swiftly on the offer given the crisis, sharpened by an Israeli security clampdown.
"This is still (a) long period," he told reporters on his return to Gaza from Egypt where he discussed the peace crisis with President Hosni Mubarak.

Palestinian legislators voted 56-1 on Thursday to give Arafat one month to replace his cabinet after a report from a panel of nine legislators detailing instances of alleged corruption and squandering of funds.
"It is a good gesture by the Palestinian Legislative Council and they should insist that their efforts are not going to be lost with the wind," a teacher from Gaza, Khaled Hassan, said.

The Palestinian Authority's legitimacy since its establishment under Israeli-PLO interim peace deals has taken a dent with ordinary Palestinians grappling with economic hardship while some officials live in relative luxury.
"They are like thiefs and changing them would be very useful but I do not believe that Arafat will replace them," said Yakub Jaarah, 60, as he played dice with friends in Ramallah.
Some cabinet ministers also doubted that Arafat would act soon.
"The president desires to postpone the issue for the time being because of the very difficult circumstances in the political process," Telecommunications Minister Imad al-Falouji said.
Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo, a close confidant of Arafat and one of the two ministers not to offer to quit, said the gesture by his colleagues was "meaningless".
"Even if new highly qualified ministers were appointed, if the management of the Authority continues as it is now these people will not be able to make any changes," he told Reuters.
"There should be a slow and deep treatment of the real problems that the Palestinian Authority departments suffer from. crucial changes have to take place and not just cosmetic ones," he said.

The legislators' report recommended putting on trial two ministers, Civilian Affairs Minister Jamil al-Tarifi and Planning Minister Nabil Shaath, who was not at Friday's cabinet, on suspicion of corruption and misue of funds.
Both have called the allegations slander.
"It is a catastrophe for the people to discover that they may have been ruled by corrupt officials," said Iatidal Aqel, a 34-year-old businesswoman from Gaza.
An official auditor's report earlier this year found the Palestinian Authority had squandered $326 million in 1996, much of it foreign aid. It did not investigate Arafat's office.

The report's findings were the subject of an investigation by a committee appointed by Arafat which reported last week that while money had not been squandered, serious financial, legal and administrative violations had taken place.
